title: The history of combustion and conservation of mass
tagline: From a million-year-old campfire to the Keeling Curve: how people learned that burning destroys nothing.
intro: People used fire for a million years before anyone knew what it was. For most of the 1700s chemists believed burning released a fire substance called phlogiston. Then scientists started weighing everything, in sealed vessels, and found the opposite: burning takes in part of the air, and not a speck of matter is lost.

eras.name: Fire before chemistry
eras.summary: Early humans learn to keep and use fire long before anyone can say what a flame is.

eras.name: Fire as a substance
eras.summary: Chemists explain burning with phlogiston, a fire stuff that escapes in the flame, while careful weighing starts to turn up awkward facts.

eras.name: The oxygen revolution
eras.summary: Oxygen is found three times over, and the Lavoisiers show with sealed vessels and balances that burning is joining with it and that mass is conserved.

eras.name: Flames at work, and their cost
eras.summary: Safety lamps, candle lectures and engines put combustion to work, and measurements show where all that carbon goes.

events.title: Ash deep inside a cave
events.text: Deep inside Wonderwerk Cave, far from the entrance, scientists found ash from burnt plants and bits of burnt bone in layers about a million years old. Tiny cracks and colours in the bone show it was heated where it lay. It is among the oldest secure signs of people using fire, though some researchers argue for older ones.
events.why: Fire gave early humans warmth, light, safety and cooked food, the first chemistry anyone ever controlled.

events.title: Fire at the Peking Man cave?
events.who: Homo erectus ("Peking Man"); dug up from the 1920s
events.text: Burnt bones and thick dark layers in the Zhoukoudian caves were long taken as the hearths of Peking Man. A careful study in 1998 found burnt bone but no clear ash or hearths, so whether these people kept fires there is still argued about.
events.why: It shows how hard it is to prove who first tamed fire, and why old claims need testing.

events.title: Metals that get heavier in the fire
events.text: Boyle heated lead and tin in sealed glass vessels. When he opened them and weighed the metal's ash, called a calx, it was heavier than the metal. He guessed that particles of fire had passed through the glass and stuck to it.
events.why: A real clue, misread: he opened the vessel before weighing, so air rushed in and the extra weight was really oxygen.

events.title: Phlogiston: fire as a substance
events.text: Building on Johann Becher's ideas, Stahl taught that everything that burns holds a fire substance, phlogiston, which escapes in the flame. Charcoal was almost pure phlogiston; a metal was its calx plus phlogiston. The idea explained a lot and ruled chemistry for most of the century.
events.why: It was the first big theory of burning, and it was wrong in a way that pushed chemists to start weighing things.

events.title: Fixed air: carbon dioxide is found
events.text: Black heated magnesia alba and chalk and weighed them. They lost weight by giving off a gas he called fixed air, the gas we call carbon dioxide. He later found it in the breath and in the gases from burning charcoal.
events.why: Careful weighing showed that a gas could be part of a solid, and gave chemists the first product of burning.

events.title: Lomonosov's sealed flasks
events.text: Lomonosov repeated Boyle's test but kept the flasks sealed. Heating metal inside them did not change the total weight; only letting air in did. He had already written to Leonhard Euler in 1748 that matter lost in one place is gained in another. His results were recorded in his notes and were little known in Western Europe.
events.why: He reached the conservation of mass years before Lavoisier, though historians still debate how complete his proof was.

events.title: Scheele makes "fire air"
events.text: Scheele, a pharmacist, heated mercury oxide, saltpetre and other substances and collected a gas that made things burn fiercely. He called it fire air. His book describing it was held up at the printer until 1777, so others were credited first.
events.why: He was probably the first to make oxygen, a reminder that discoveries often happen twice.

events.title: Priestley's candle burns brighter
events.text: Priestley focused sunlight with a large lens onto red mercury calx. A gas came off in which a candle burned with a dazzling flame and a mouse lived longer than in ordinary air. He called it dephlogisticated air and told Lavoisier about it in Paris that October.
events.why: Priestley found oxygen but kept the phlogiston theory; Lavoisier saw what it really meant.

events.title: Tin in a sealed retort
events.text: Lavoisier heated tin in sealed glass vessels and weighed everything before and after. The total did not change. When he broke the seal, air rushed in, and the weight rose by exactly what the tin had gained.
events.why: The metal was taking something out of the air, not losing phlogiston: the key experiment behind this box's first chapter.

events.title: A new theory of burning
events.text: In a paper on combustion in general, Lavoisier argued that burning, rusting and breathing are all a substance joining with part of the air. He named that part oxygène, "acid maker", because he wrongly thought all acids contained it.
events.why: It replaced phlogiston with the idea we still use: burning is joining with oxygen.

events.title: Breathing is slow burning
events.text: Lavoisier and Laplace put a guinea pig in an ice calorimeter and measured the heat it gave out and the fixed air it breathed out. Burning charcoal to make the same amount of that gas gave nearly the same heat. Breathing, they concluded, is a slow combustion.
events.why: It linked the flame and the body, the idea behind this box's chapter on fat and breath.

events.title: Marie-Anne Lavoisier answers the phlogistonists
events.text: Marie-Anne Lavoisier translated Richard Kirwan's Essay on Phlogiston from English into French, adding notes that took its arguments apart. She kept the laboratory's records, took part in experiments and hosted scientists from across Europe.
events.why: Her work spread the new chemistry, though she was rarely credited in her lifetime.

events.title: The law in a textbook
events.who: Antoine Lavoisier, with drawings by Marie-Anne Lavoisier
events.text: Lavoisier's Traité élémentaire de chimie stated that nothing is created in any operation, of art or of nature: the same quantity of matter exists before and after. It listed 33 elements and used a new, logical naming system. Marie-Anne drew its 13 plates of apparatus. Five years later Lavoisier was guillotined in the Revolution.
events.why: It is often called the first modern chemistry textbook, and it made conservation of mass the ground rule of chemistry.

events.title: A flame that can't escape
events.text: Coal mines were full of firedamp, methane, which exploded when miners' candles lit it. Davy wrapped the flame in fine iron gauze. The gauze soaks up heat so fast that flame can't pass through it to the gas outside.
events.why: It saved many lives, and showed that a flame needs heat as well as fuel and oxygen.

events.title: The Chemical History of a Candle
events.text: In Christmas lectures for young people, Faraday burned candles and caught what came off. He showed that the wax turns into water and carbon dioxide, using oxygen from the air, and that we do the same when we breathe. He gave the lectures again in 1860, and they became a famous book.
events.why: It is still one of the best explanations of combustion ever written for young people.

events.title: The four-stroke engine
events.text: Otto built an engine that sucked in fuel and air, squeezed it, burned it and pushed out the exhaust, in four strokes of the piston. Squeezing the mixture before lighting it made it far more efficient than earlier gas engines.
events.why: Nearly every petrol car and motorbike engine still works this way.

events.title: Energy has mass
events.text: In a short paper, Einstein showed that anything that gives out energy E loses mass E ÷ c². For burning, the loss is about one part in ten billion, far too small to weigh.
events.why: It is the one tiny exception to Lavoisier's law, and it matters only in nuclear reactions.

events.title: Measuring the CO₂ we make
events.text: Keeling began measuring carbon dioxide in the air with great precision, high on a Hawaiian volcano. His record, the Keeling Curve, rises every year, with a small wobble as plants grow and die with the seasons.
events.why: It shows the conservation of mass on a planetary scale: the carbon we burn does not vanish, it stays in the air.

events.title: Catalytic converters arrive
events.who: Carmakers, under the US Clean Air Act
events.text: From the 1975 models, most new petrol cars in the US got catalytic converters to meet new limits on carbon monoxide and unburnt fuel. They needed unleaded petrol, because lead ruins the catalyst. Three-way converters that also clean NOx followed a few years later.
events.why: They cut the poisons from incomplete burning, though every gram of fuel carbon still leaves as CO₂.

events.title: Where does lost fat go?
events.where: University of New South Wales, Sydney
events.text: Meerman, a physicist, and Brown, a chemist, followed every atom in 10 kg of body fat as it is burned. They found that 8.4 kg leaves as carbon dioxide through the lungs and 1.6 kg as water. Many doctors and trainers they surveyed had guessed it turned into energy or heat.
events.why: It is Lavoisier's law applied to your own body: mass lost has to go somewhere.

people.name: Antoine Lavoisier
people.note: Weighed everything, named oxygen and hydrogen, and made conservation of mass the ground rule of chemistry.

people.name: Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier
people.note: Worked beside Antoine in the lab, translated and rebutted the phlogistonists, and drew the plates of his Traité.

people.name: Mikhail Lomonosov
people.role: Scientist, poet and founder of Moscow University
people.note: Showed in 1756 that metals heated in sealed flasks don't change the total weight.

people.name: Joseph Priestley
people.note: Discovered oxygen in 1774 but defended phlogiston to the end of his life.

people.name: Carl Wilhelm Scheele
people.note: Made oxygen first, around 1771–72, but his book came out too late for the credit.

people.name: Joseph Black
people.note: Found fixed air, carbon dioxide, by weighing what solids lose when heated.

people.name: Michael Faraday
people.note: Explained a burning candle to children so well that his lectures are still in print.

series.title: Carbon dioxide in the air at Mauna Loa, Hawaii
series.caption: Every tonne of carbon we burn leaves as about 3.7 tonnes of CO₂, and much of it stays in the air. Data: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory.

facts: Burning 1 kg of carbon makes 3.67 kg of carbon dioxide, because each carbon atom picks up two oxygen atoms from the air.
Priestley told Lavoisier about his new gas over dinner in Paris in October 1774. Lavoisier understood it better than Priestley did.
Antoine Lavoisier was also a tax collector for the king. That job, not his chemistry, got him guillotined in 1794, during the French Revolution.
Most of the mass you lose when you slim down leaves through your lungs, as carbon dioxide.
Einstein's E = mc² means a burning fuel does lose mass, but only about one part in ten billion: no balance has ever seen it.
